behavioral.title: Behavioral Question Bank
behavioral.description: Common behavioral prompts with what each one is really testing and how to frame a STAR answer.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate. How did you resolve it?
questions.assesses: Whether you can disagree on substance without making it personal, and reach a decision the team commits to.
questions.starTip: Situation: the technical decision at stake. Task: your stake in it. Action: how you surfaced data and heard them out. Result: the decision made and that the relationship held.

questions.prompt: Describe a project that failed or missed its goal. What did you learn?
questions.assesses: Ownership over blame-shifting, and whether you extract a concrete, applied lesson.
questions.starTip: Pick a real miss you owned. Keep the setup short, be specific about your contribution to the failure, and end on the changed behavior — not a vague 'I learned to communicate more'.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you led without formal authority.
questions.assesses: Influence, initiative, and whether people follow you because of trust rather than a title.
questions.starTip: Show you saw a gap, rallied people around a plan, and drove it to a result. Quantify the impact and name what others contributed.

questions.prompt: Give an example of working under a tight deadline with shifting requirements.
questions.assesses: How you prioritize and stay effective when the target moves — scoping, not heroics.
questions.starTip: Emphasize how you cut scope to the essential, communicated trade-offs early, and still shipped something valuable on time.

questions.prompt: Describe a time you received difficult feedback. What did you do with it?
questions.assesses: Coachability and self-awareness — do you act on feedback or defend against it?
questions.starTip: State the feedback plainly, resist justifying, then show the specific change you made and evidence it stuck.

questions.prompt: Tell me about your most significant technical contribution and its impact.
questions.assesses: Scope of ownership and whether you measure your work by outcomes, not effort.
questions.starTip: Lead with the business or user result, then explain the technical decision that drove it. Numbers beat adjectives.

questions.prompt: Describe a time you had to convince stakeholders to change direction.
questions.assesses: Communicating trade-offs to non-experts and building buy-in without authority.
questions.starTip: Frame their concern first, present the evidence in their terms (cost, risk, timeline), and show how you reached alignment.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to learn something unfamiliar quickly to deliver.
questions.assesses: Learning velocity and how you de-risk the unknown under time pressure.
questions.starTip: Show your approach to ramping fast — narrowing to what you needed, leaning on the right sources — and that it produced a shipped result.

questions.prompt: Describe a production incident you were involved in. What was your role?
questions.assesses: Behaviour under pressure, and whether you separate mitigation from root cause.
questions.starTip: Stop the bleeding first, then diagnose — say it in that order. End with the durable fix and the guardrail (alert, test, runbook) that stops a repeat.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a technical decision you made that you would make differently today.
questions.assesses: Honest retrospection and whether your judgment has actually improved.
questions.starTip: Give the constraints you had at the time so the decision sounds reasonable, then name the signal you now know to weigh more heavily.

questions.prompt: Describe a time you had to say no to a request from a stakeholder.
questions.assesses: Whether you defend focus with reasons rather than either caving or stonewalling.
questions.starTip: Show the trade-off explicitly — what would have been dropped — and that you offered an alternative or a timeline rather than a flat refusal.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you improved a process or tool for your team.
questions.assesses: Whether you fix systemic friction or just route around it personally.
questions.starTip: Quantify the before and after — build minutes, on-call pages, review latency — and mention adoption, since a tool nobody uses is not an improvement.

questions.prompt: Describe a time you mentored someone or unblocked a struggling teammate.
questions.assesses: Whether you scale through others or hoard the interesting work.
questions.starTip: Show that you diagnosed what they were missing rather than taking the keyboard, and point to what they could do afterwards without you.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to make a decision without enough data.
questions.assesses: Comfort with reversible risk and whether you make the uncertainty explicit.
questions.starTip: Name what you knew, what you assumed, and the cheapest experiment that would have proved you wrong. Say how you set a point to revisit the call.

questions.prompt: Describe a project where you had to work across teams with competing priorities.
questions.assesses: Whether you can align incentives, not just escalate.
questions.starTip: Show you found the shared goal, made the dependency and its cost visible early, and kept the other team informed rather than surprised.

questions.prompt: Tell me about the most complex system you have worked on. How did you get up to speed?
questions.assesses: Genuine technical depth — a shallow answer collapses under two follow-ups.
questions.starTip: Pick something you can whiteboard. Explain the design, the part you owned, and one trade-off the system made, including what it gave up.

questions.prompt: Describe a time you pushed back on a deadline or a scope you thought was unrealistic.
questions.assesses: Whether you raise risk early with evidence, or silently absorb it until it explodes.
questions.starTip: Emphasise timing — you raised it before the crunch — and that you came with options (cut scope, add people, move the date) rather than only a problem.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you shipped something and the outcome was not what you expected.
questions.assesses: Whether you measure after shipping, and how you react to a disappointing metric.
questions.starTip: Show the instrumentation was in place before launch, what the data said, and the decision that followed — iterate, roll back, or kill it.

questions.prompt: Why are you looking to leave your current role, and what are you looking for next?
questions.assesses: Self-knowledge and whether this role actually matches what you want.
questions.starTip: Keep it forward-looking and specific to what this team does. Criticising your current employer costs you more than any story it buys.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision but had to commit to it anyway.
questions.assesses: Disagree-and-commit — whether the disagreement ends when the decision is made.
questions.starTip: Show you argued the case once, clearly, then executed without hedging. Say how you kept a way to revisit it if the evidence changed.

systemDesign.title: System Design Primer
systemDesign.description: How to drive a design round, plus the building blocks you'll assemble — and when each one earns its place.

framework.title: Clarify requirements
framework.detail: Pin down functional needs and non-functional targets (scale, latency, availability) before drawing anything. Ask; don't assume.

framework.title: Estimate scale
framework.detail: Back-of-envelope the QPS, data volume, and bandwidth. The numbers decide whether one box or a fleet is the answer.

framework.title: Sketch the API
framework.detail: Name the core endpoints and their inputs/outputs. It anchors the rest of the design in concrete operations.

framework.title: Design the data model
framework.detail: Choose storage and schema for the access patterns — reads vs writes, relational vs key-value, hot vs cold.

framework.title: Scale and defend
framework.detail: Add caching, replication, sharding, and queues where the numbers demand them, and state the trade-offs you're accepting.

concepts.name: Load Balancer
concepts.summary: Spreads incoming requests across a pool of servers and routes around unhealthy ones.
concepts.whenToUse: Any time you scale horizontally — it removes the single-server hotspot and enables rolling deploys.

concepts.name: Caching
concepts.summary: Keeps hot data in fast storage (in-memory / CDN) close to where it's read.
concepts.whenToUse: Read-heavy workloads with repeated queries. The hard part is invalidation — decide TTL vs write-through up front.

concepts.name: Database Sharding
concepts.summary: Partitions data across nodes by a shard key so no single database holds everything.
concepts.whenToUse: When one database can't hold the volume or serve the write throughput. Pick a key that spreads load evenly.

concepts.name: Replication
concepts.summary: Maintains copies of data for failover and read scaling (leader/follower or multi-leader).
concepts.whenToUse: High availability and read-heavy scaling. Accept that followers lag — reads may be slightly stale.

concepts.name: Message Queue
concepts.summary: Decouples producers from consumers, buffering work to be processed asynchronously.
concepts.whenToUse: Spiky load, long-running or async tasks, and smoothing bursts so downstream systems aren't overwhelmed.

concepts.name: CAP Theorem
concepts.summary: Under a network partition you can keep either consistency or availability, not both.
concepts.whenToUse: Framing the core trade-off. Partitions are inevitable, so state whether the system is CP or AP and why.

concepts.name: CDN
concepts.summary: Edge servers cache static assets geographically close to users.
concepts.whenToUse: Global delivery of static or media content — cuts latency and offloads origin bandwidth.

concepts.name: Rate Limiting
concepts.summary: Caps how many requests a client may make in a window (token bucket, sliding window).
concepts.whenToUse: Protecting the system from abuse, runaway clients, and thundering-herd overload.

concepts.name: Consistent Hashing
concepts.summary: Maps keys to nodes on a ring so adding/removing a node reshuffles only a small slice of keys.
concepts.whenToUse: Distributed caches and shard routing where nodes come and go without a full rebalance.

concepts.name: Indexing
concepts.summary: A secondary structure that speeds lookups at the cost of extra writes and space.
concepts.whenToUse: Frequent reads that filter or sort on a column. Every index you add taxes writes — don't over-index.

concepts.name: Idempotency
concepts.summary: A repeated request has the same effect as a single one, usually via a client-supplied key.
concepts.whenToUse: Anywhere retries exist — payments, webhooks, queue consumers. It is what makes at-least-once delivery survivable.

concepts.name: Circuit Breaker
concepts.summary: Stops calling a failing dependency for a cooling-off period instead of retrying into the fire.
concepts.whenToUse: Any synchronous call to a service that can degrade. Without it, retries turn one slow dependency into a cascading outage.

concepts.name: Write-Ahead Log
concepts.summary: Appends every change to a durable sequential log before applying it to the main structure.
concepts.whenToUse: Durability and crash recovery, and the same log doubles as the replication stream and a change-data-capture feed.

concepts.name: Leader Election
concepts.summary: Consensus (Raft/Paxos, or a coordination service) picks one node to accept writes.
concepts.whenToUse: Any replicated store or scheduler that needs a single writer. State how a failover is detected and what happens to in-flight writes.

concepts.name: Blob Store + Metadata DB
concepts.summary: Large objects live in object storage; the database holds only pointers and attributes.
concepts.whenToUse: Media, uploads and attachments. Keeping megabyte payloads out of the primary database is what keeps its working set cacheable.

concepts.name: Fan-out on Write vs Read
concepts.summary: Push a new item into every follower's feed at write time, or assemble the feed per request.
concepts.whenToUse: Feed and notification designs. Write fan-out gives fast reads but explodes for celebrity accounts — real systems mix both.

concepts.name: Backpressure
concepts.summary: Signals producers to slow down when consumers or queues fall behind, instead of buffering forever.
concepts.whenToUse: Any pipeline with variable load. Without it, an unbounded queue converts a throughput problem into an out-of-memory crash.

concepts.name: Bloom Filter
concepts.summary: A compact probabilistic membership test: no false negatives, some false positives.
concepts.whenToUse: Skipping expensive lookups — checking whether an SSTable or a cache could possibly hold a key before reading it.

systemDesign.title: ML System Design Primer
systemDesign.description: How to drive an ML design round — framing the problem, shaping the data, serving the model, and catching it when it rots.

framework.title: Frame it as an ML problem
framework.detail: State the business goal, then the ML formulation: what is predicted, at what granularity, and what a single training example looks like. Ask whether ML is warranted at all — many rounds reward proposing a rules baseline first.

framework.title: Define labels and the offline metric
framework.detail: Where does ground truth come from, and how delayed is it? Choose a metric that survives class imbalance, and separate it from the online metric the business actually cares about.

framework.title: Design the data and features
framework.detail: Sources, volume, freshness, and how features are computed. Name which are batch and which are real time, and how the same code serves both — training/serving skew is the classic failure.

framework.title: Pick a model and a baseline
framework.detail: Start simple — logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees — and justify anything heavier by the data volume and latency budget. State how you would split train, validation and test without leakage.

framework.title: Serve it
framework.detail: Batch scoring versus online inference, latency budget, caching, and how the model is versioned and rolled back. Say where the model runs and what happens when it is unavailable.

framework.title: Monitor and retrain
framework.detail: Track input drift, prediction distribution and the online metric. Decide the retraining trigger and how new models are validated — shadow traffic, then A/B, then ramp.

concepts.name: Feature Store
concepts.summary: A shared store of computed features, serving the same definitions to training and inference.
concepts.whenToUse: Whenever features are non-trivial or reused across models. Its main job is eliminating training/serving skew.

concepts.name: Training/Serving Skew
concepts.summary: The gap between how a feature is computed offline and online — different code, different time windows, different nulls.
concepts.whenToUse: Name it explicitly in any design round; it is the most common reason a strong offline model underperforms in production.

concepts.name: Data Leakage
concepts.summary: Information unavailable at prediction time leaking into training, inflating offline scores.
concepts.whenToUse: Guard by splitting before any fitting, and by splitting on time for anything with a temporal ordering.

concepts.name: Offline vs Online Metric
concepts.summary: AUC or F1 measured on held-out data versus click-through, revenue or retention measured live.
concepts.whenToUse: Always state both and how they connect. A model can improve offline and hurt the online metric.

concepts.name: Batch vs Online Inference
concepts.summary: Precomputing predictions on a schedule versus computing them per request.
concepts.whenToUse: Batch when the input set is known and latency is loose; online when inputs arrive per request or freshness matters.

concepts.name: Model Registry & Versioning
concepts.summary: Tracks model artifacts with their training data, code and metrics, so any deployed model is reproducible.
concepts.whenToUse: Needed the moment more than one model version exists — it is what makes rollback possible.

concepts.name: Shadow Deployment
concepts.summary: Runs the new model on live traffic without using its output, purely to compare.
concepts.whenToUse: Before any risky rollout — it surfaces latency and skew problems with no user impact.

concepts.name: Drift Detection
concepts.summary: Watches input feature distributions and prediction distributions for change over time.
concepts.whenToUse: Any long-lived model. Data drift precedes accuracy loss, and it is visible without waiting for labels.

concepts.name: Feedback Loop
concepts.summary: The model's own predictions shape the data it later trains on — recommendations create the clicks they learn from.
concepts.whenToUse: Call it out in ranking and recommendation designs, and propose exploration or randomised holdouts to break it.

concepts.name: Two-Stage Retrieval & Ranking
concepts.summary: A cheap model retrieves a few hundred candidates from millions; an expensive model ranks them.
concepts.whenToUse: Any recommendation or search design — scoring the whole catalogue per request is infeasible under a latency budget.

concepts.name: Cold Start
concepts.summary: New users or items have no interaction history for the model to use.
concepts.whenToUse: Recommenders and personalisation. Fall back to content features or popularity until signal accumulates.

concepts.name: Quantisation & Distillation
concepts.summary: Shrinking a model by lowering numeric precision or training a small model to imitate a large one.
concepts.whenToUse: When the latency or cost budget will not fit the model that scores best offline.

concepts.name: Label Delay & Proxy Labels
concepts.summary: Ground truth that arrives days later (a chargeback, a churn event), so a proxy signal stands in meanwhile.
concepts.whenToUse: Fraud, churn and long-horizon predictions. Say how long the delay is and what the proxy costs you in bias.

concepts.name: Class Imbalance Handling
concepts.summary: Resampling, class weights or threshold tuning when positives are a fraction of a percent.
concepts.whenToUse: Fraud, spam, rare-disease and safety models. Always pair it with a metric that survives imbalance — never accuracy.

concepts.name: Embedding Store & ANN Index
concepts.summary: Vectors served through an approximate nearest-neighbour index (HNSW, IVF) rather than exact search.
concepts.whenToUse: Retrieval, semantic search and RAG. Name the recall/latency knob and how the index is rebuilt as embeddings change.

concepts.name: Human-in-the-Loop Review
concepts.summary: Low-confidence or high-impact predictions route to a reviewer, whose decisions become training labels.
concepts.whenToUse: Moderation, medical and financial decisions. It gives both a safety net and a cheap stream of high-quality labels.

concepts.name: Guardrails & Fallbacks
concepts.summary: Rules, filters and a default response wrapping the model for when it is wrong, slow or unavailable.
concepts.whenToUse: Any user-facing model, and mandatory for LLM designs. State what the system returns when inference times out.

concepts.name: Experiment Design (A/B)
concepts.summary: Randomised assignment, a pre-declared primary metric, and enough traffic to detect the expected effect.
concepts.whenToUse: Every model rollout. Bring up sample size, guardrail metrics and the risk of peeking at results early.
